t: Research
x: Research I study how artificial intelligence changes the way a company is managed: not individual tasks, but the system itself — planning, decision-making, control and communication. It's a continuation of my product work: by day I build a service with an AI agent at a bank, and in my research I try to understand why such projects work in some companies and fail in others. PhD programme at RANEPA · 2024–2027 · Institute of Industry Management, Department of Theory and Systems of Industry Management “Using artificial intelligence to improve a company's management system” 3 articles in peer-reviewed journals (VAK list) 3 talks at international conferences How I do research Besides reviewing the literature and company practice, the empirical part of the dissertation is a case study at a large Russian bank. I ran a series of semi-structured interviews with four groups of respondents: AI product and project managers, specialists from the AI technology centre, top management, and employees who work with AI tools every day. The interviews are anonymised, and the answers are compiled into a thematic matrix: where AI is built into management, how goals and KPIs for adoption are set, what gets in the way and what helps. The summary is in the post “What holds AI back in management” . Questions I'm interested in In which management processes AI really makes a difference, and where it's just hype. What risks and limitations it brings — from data quality to accountability for a decision. What a company needs to prepare in advance: data, infrastructure, people and rules. t: About me
x: About me Hi 👋 This page is a short manual for working with me. It's for colleagues, teammates and anyone I'm starting something with: so we spend less time getting used to each other and more time on the product . What I do By day I'm a product manager, and as a PhD student at RANEPA I'm writing a dissertation on “Using artificial intelligence to improve a company's management system” . It's the same topic from two sides: at work I build a service with an AI agent for credit analysis, and in my research I look at how AI changes not individual tasks but management itself — planning, decision-making, control and communication inside a company. I'm interested in three questions: in which management processes AI really makes a difference, and where it's just hype; what risks and limitations it brings — from data quality to accountability for a decision; what a company needs to prepare in advance: data, infrastructure, people and rules. That's what my articles and talks are about, and I cover the practical side in the AI agents section. What I believe in Hypothesis → test → decision One primary metric per experiment Business results matter more than the number of features AI strengthens management but doesn't take responsibility away from people Process and data first, the model second AI where it delivers measurable value, not AI for its own sake How to work with me I start with “why”. Before discussing a solution, I'll ask which user or business problem we're solving and how we'll know we've solved it. It's not distrust, it's a habit. I like numbers and facts. An opinion without data is a fine starting point, but I want to make decisions based on customer interviews, analytics or an experiment. Sober about AI. If you suggest “adding AI”, I'll ask which process it will improve, how we'll measure the effect and who is responsible when the model is wrong. If there are answers, I'm the first to support it. Feedback — directly. If something is wrong with the product, the process or my work, tell me right away and to the point. I give feedback the same way: specifically, with a suggestion for what to change. Bad news — early. A missed deadline I learn about a week ahead is plan B. The same deadline I learn about on release day is a fire. Communication. I reply fastest on Telegram. I read email, but not instantly. If it's urgent, say so. Meetings. A meeting needs a goal and an outcome: at the end we write down who does what and by when. If you're unsure whether to message me — message me. t: What holds AI back in management — findings from interviews at a large bank
x: What holds AI back in management — findings from interviews at a large bank For the empirical part of my PhD I ran a series of semi-structured interviews inside a large Russian bank. The question is simple: how does AI actually get built into a company's management system — and what gets in the way? Below are generalised findings, without the bank's name, people's names or internal figures. The case Object. A large Russian bank with a wide branch network, moving from isolated pilots to systematic use of AI. Who I interviewed. Four groups of respondents: product and project managers who implement AI initiatives; specialists from the AI technology centre; top management; employees who use AI tools in their work. How. One interview guide: a common block for everyone and a specialised block per role. Interviews are anonymised, key quotes extracted, answers coded into a thematic matrix — which themes repeat across groups. How AI is governed A dedicated structure above departments. There's an AI centre with its own strategy and a data management function next to it. Strategic goals and adoption KPIs are set at the top and cascade down to department heads. Initiatives come from the business. A unit brings a problem; together with the AI centre it's turned into an AI task with a target metric. Business units have "AI advocates" — people who know the processes and understand what AI can and can't do. Selection by three criteria: economic effect, data readiness and process repeatability. If the effect is large but the data isn't ready, the initiative becomes "preparatory": fix data and processes first, then pilot. Accountability stays with the business. If AI scoring is built into the lending process, the risk manager owns the decision. AI is a tool, not the accountable party. Where AI already works Maturity differs a lot by area. Classic machine learning has long been in production: anti-fraud, scoring, speech analytics in the contact centre. Generative AI is moving from pilots to scale: internal assistants for staff, document summarisation, drafts of analytical reports. Agentic systems are at an early pilot stage. Five barriers Process, not the model. The most common answer: the blocker isn't model accuracy but the lack of a business process where the output becomes a step rather than "one more dashboard for reference". It's an organisational problem, and it's slow to fix because it touches people's areas of responsibility. Data. In a pilot the data is pulled by hand; production needs an automated pipeline — and it turns out sources update at the wrong frequency and have no availability guarantees. People and trust. Employees either blindly trust the model's suggestion — making its error their error — or ignore it. A tool can be technically available for months while only a small share of staff use it. Plus a shortage of specialists and dependence on a few experts. Line managers. Adoption hinges on line managers: if they don't understand what AI can and can't do, "pseudo-AI" initiatives appear and real opportunities are missed. Regulation and security. Customers' personal data rules out external models — you need a closed environment, which limits model choice. Final decisions need explainability and a fallback: why the model decided this and how to challenge it. Models drift with the portfolio and the economy and need constant monitoring. Takeaways Autonomous AI-based management decisions are unacceptable in a bank today. The model is an adviser: it collects and structures information, highlights risks, double-checks data. The decision stays with a human. A gap between the model and the decision is normal, not a failure. The model optimises one objective; a management decision balances several, some of which can't be formalised. Start narrow. An example from the interviews: instead of a churn model for the whole portfolio, it was launched for one segment and one channel where data and a retention process already existed. A smaller but measurable and fast effect — and the right to scale. If you change one thing — build AI literacy into line managers' planning and create a single platform of reusable components so a new initiative launches in weeks, not months. What it means for a product manager Almost all barriers are product problems, not technical ones: which process the output plugs into, who owns it, how users know when to trust the model, which metric defines success. I follow the same principles building a service with an AI agent at work and in my own AI projects . More about the PhD on the research page. I wrote about AI risks in banks in an article and a talk .

t: "Inspired" by Marty Cagan: the essentials of product management
x: "Inspired" by Marty Cagan: the essentials of product management 10 /10 — my rating Key ideas from the core book on the product manager's job: how strong product teams differ from "feature factories" and why most ideas don't work the first time. Marty Cagan is a former product leader at eBay, Netscape and HP and the founder of Silicon Valley Product Group. "Inspired" is his book on how technology companies create products customers love. Below is what I took from it and use at work and in my course. Most ideas won't work The book's main idea: at least half of our ideas won't deliver, and those that do will need several iterations. So a strong team doesn't "deliver the roadmap" — it quickly and cheaply filters out bad ideas before engineering time is spent on them. Four risks Before building, the team tests four risks: Value — will people buy it or use it? Usability — can users figure out how to use it? Feasibility — can we build it in reasonable time and budget? Business viability — does it work for the business: legal, sales, finance, brand? The product manager owns value and viability, the designer usability, the tech lead feasibility. Discovery and Delivery A product team works on two parallel tracks. Discovery — figuring out what's worth building: interviews, prototypes, quick experiments. Delivery — building it well and shipping. Many companies only do the second. I gave this pair its own slide in the first lecture of my IT management course. Prototypes instead of specs Instead of long requirements, Cagan suggests testing ideas with prototypes: from a clickable mockup to a "Wizard of Oz", where a human works behind the interface by hand. A prototype costs days, not months, and answers "do we need this?" before development. Missionaries, not mercenaries A mercenary team does what it's told. A missionary team gets a problem and owns the outcome — that the solution works, not just that it shipped. For that, the team needs context: product vision, strategy and clear goals. Who the product manager is For Cagan, the PM owns the product's value and viability, and needs deep knowledge of four things: users, data, the business, and the market and industry. Not a "backlog owner" or project manager — the person who decides what's worth building. Who should read it Anyone working in product or planning to. For beginners it's a map of the profession; for experienced PMs, the language to explain to the business why a product team shouldn't be a feature factory. If you read one book on product management, read this one.

t: bolz.dev — an MCP connector that lets AI agents take real-world actions
x: bolz.dev — an MCP connector that lets AI agents take real-world actions In August 2025 we built the MVP of bolz.dev — a Model Context Protocol platform that lets AI agents not just recommend but finish the job: find, book and pay for real services. The problem Agents are great at search but almost always end by sending the user to a website link — "take it from here". The best models complete real-world tasks less than half the time (MCP-Universe benchmark). Buying a flight via an AI agent today takes longer than doing it yourself: the agent imitates a human — search, links, forms. On the other side are services: most companies risk not appearing in agent answers at all and losing customers. The solution Bolz Connector sits between agents and services: a service connects once — via a plugin, web interface or REST API; the agent gets normalised data, live prices and functions "search / reserve / confirm / refund / pay"; the user goes from request to payment to done in a single conversation. We designed two scenarios: a marketplace ("find a housewarming gift under $100") and taxi ("call a Comfort car and avoid traffic"). How to measure quality The key lesson: for such an agent, judging the model's answer isn't enough. Success is a completed action: a paid order, a car on its way, a purchased ticket. So we built in execution-based evals — checking the outcome, not the text. Why it matters to me bolz.dev grew out of bolz.tech, our sharing ecosystem: we saw users increasingly arrive via AI assistants rather than apps. For me it's also the most direct experience in the agent layer: MCP, agent tools, evals and metrics for agentic scenarios. I later applied the same approach in the Weekend Planner . t: My HSE master's thesis — how to tell whether digital transformation will pay off
x: My HSE master's thesis — how to tell whether digital transformation will pay off My master's thesis in the Corporate Finance programme at HSE University's Faculty of Economic Sciences was "Modelling and evaluating the efficiency of a company's digital transformation investment projects". It started the research line I now continue in my PhD at RANEPA — this time about AI. The problem Large companies invest huge sums in digital transformation, yet there are hardly any methods to forecast a project's success and estimate future benefits upfront. Existing evaluations: rely on qualitative criteria without clear ways to measure them; count only financial indicators and don't split capital and operating costs by technology area; report final effects without a calculation method, so the same indicators differ between sources. What I studied Analysed the digital transformation programmes of Rosseti ("Digital Transformation 2030"), Russian Railways ("Digital Railway") and Lukoil ("Digital Lukoil") and compared their technology bets: IoT, AI, big data, digital twins, robots and drones. Separated two concepts: digital optimisation improves existing processes, while digital transformation changes the value proposition and creates new products. Compared groups of evaluation methods — from cost accounting (TCO) to the balanced scorecard — and proposed steps for defining a project's non-financial metrics. Built a forecasting evaluation model with elements of risk scenario analysis. Four hypotheses Digital transformation projects are innovation projects and must be evaluated differently from ordinary investments: goals, timelines and costs are not fixed upfront. A company with steady growth can keep its competitive advantages for a while even without digital transformation. With outdated infrastructure, lack of funds and unprepared staff, transformation leads to wasted spending and missed results. A successful transformation project changes the business process model and makes the company more efficient. Conclusion A digital transformation project alone doesn't guarantee success. Management must understand at the review stage how realistic the project is and whether the company is ready for it at its current life-cycle stage. But ignoring digitalisation is even more dangerous: technology players take over markets. That's why a comprehensive evaluation method is needed, with non-financial metrics next to financial ones. I now study the same question — "is the company ready, and what should be prepared upfront" — for AI: see the talk on infrastructure requirements and the research page. 📎 Defence slides, PDF (in Russian)

The platform connects three sides: recipient — the person who needs help; helper — a volunteer or specialist who does the job; donor — someone who pays for the job when the helper isn't a volunteer. How it works The recipient verifies their status via Gosuslugi (government services portal) and posts a task. Helpers are notified and respond; the recipient picks one. Donors are notified; one confirms funding. The helper does the job and reports to the donor. The donor accepts the work and confirms payment. Dobster is non-profit: no commission, the donor's money goes straight to the task. Potential audience — 69 million people officially in socially vulnerable groups in Russia. Partnership programme To attract donors and helpers we created a programme for companies — "talk about good, give good, do good": tell clients and staff about Dobster, reward the most active helpers and donors, fund tasks or volunteer. Partners get a partner block on the platform and a joint PR campaign. What I did Created the product concept and roadmap. Designed the three-sided model and a recipient journey simple enough for an elderly person. Designed the partnership programme as an acquisition channel. Built mockups, assembled the team, launched to production. What this case shows A full launch in the social sector, where users are not the most digital audience and every transaction closes three sides at once. What I learned When three parties close a deal, each one's journey has to be designed separately. The hardest journey is the client's — an elderly person's. Attracting donors and helpers is a product in itself: that's how the partnership programme appeared. Next case: Process automation for a government department (B2G)

x: bolz.dev: an MCP connector that lets AI agents take real-world actions Key result MVP in August 2025 Role Co-founder & CPO Where bolz.dev When 2025 (startup) Product a Model Context Protocol (MCP) platform: services connect once, and AI agents find, book and pay for them on the user's behalf Stage MVP built in August 2025 Models B2B (services and e-commerce) and B2C (AI assistant users) Predecessor bolz.tech — sharing ecosystem Problem AI agents can search and recommend, but rarely finish the job: Agents: almost always send the user to a website link to complete the action; the best models succeed at real-world tasks less than half the time (MCP-Universe benchmark). Services: most companies risk not appearing in agent answers at all. Users: buying a flight via an AI agent today takes longer than doing it yourself — the agent imitates a human: search, links, forms. Solution Bolz Connector sits between agents and services: services connect once via plugins, a web interface or REST API; agents get normalised JSON, live prices and functions "search / reserve / confirm / refund / pay"; users go from request to payment in a single conversation. We designed two scenarios — a marketplace ("find a housewarming gift under $100") and taxi ("call a Comfort car, avoid traffic"). Quality is measured with execution-based evals: success is a completed action, not a model's answer. What I did as CPO Framed the problem from three sides — services, agents, users — and the value proposition for each. Designed user flows from chat request to confirmed payment. Described the architecture: agent → MCP server with service connectors → action → result check. Analysed competitors: direct (Notte, Firecrawl) and indirect (Google's own AI services, Grab, Loman.ai). Built the go-to-market: connector in Claude and ChatGPT, API integrations, sandbox and tutorials for developers. What this case shows A product at the core of the agent layer: MCP, agent tools, outcome-based evaluation and product metrics for agentic scenarios. What I learned Agent quality should be measured by the completed action (a paid order), not by the text of the answer. The value has to be framed for three sides at once: services, agents and users.
